A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renaming and relocation.

before.justification: Section 5, Figure 2 and Table 1 report original uncertainty-quantification experiments with Fourier neural operators on KdV, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Burgers equations.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original PDE experiments, including low-data evaluations, distribution shifts, autoregressive rollouts and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The core Gaussian linearization and last-Fourier-block construction are retained under the name LUNO. Appendix A.4 adds an abstract-Banach adaptation using separating linear functionals instead of point evaluations, including a bidual fallback when the output process cannot be constructed in the original space.

E1.justification: Burgers and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky remain, while KdV is removed and Hyper-Diffusion is added. V2 also evaluates two-dimensional advection-diffusion-reaction problems with velocity reversals and heat sources/sinks, plus autoregressive scenarios with accumulating prediction errors.

E2.justification: V1 compares NOLA against input and weight perturbations. V2 retains these comparator types, with weight perturbations corresponding to Sample-Iso, and adds deep ensembles, Sample-LA and the LUNO-Iso variant. Tables 1 and 4–6 establish these additions despite inconsistent labels in Tables 7 and 11.

E3.justification: The low-data protocol changes from 32/64/128 training trajectories to 25, twenty-input/twenty-output prediction to ten-input/one-output prediction, and 16 modes/32 hidden channels to 12/18. Evaluation increases from 100 to 250 test samples, and v2 adds 50-trajectory rollout evaluations. The Q statistic is retained under the chi-squared terminology.

E4.justification: V2 removes the training-size sweep but adds matched sampling-versus-linearization comparisons, covariance and eigenfunction visualizations, ensemble null-space error analysis, distribution-shift and rollout robustness tests, and runtime comparisons. Figures 2–4 and 6–7 substantially extend v1's single KdV prediction illustration.

E5.justification: Sampling-based uncertainty estimation uses 200 predictions instead of 100, and v2 specifies ten differently seeded ensemble members. Table 12 introduces runtime values with ± terms, without defining those terms or the repetition count. Main performance tables still lack uncertainty across repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: V1's three-training-size results are replaced by results under revised settings, with additional OOD, rollout and timing outcomes. V2 Table 1 reports Burgers NLL of -2.0787 for LUNO-LA versus -0.8145 for ensembles; Table 2 instead favors ensembles on Pos-Neg-Flip (-1.014 versus 1.164). These are new comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: V1's Banach-valued Gaussian currying theory is substantially generalized to random processes on vector spaces, including non-Gaussian cases and new measurability/separation results. Appendix A adds weak Gâteaux differentiability, bidual constructions, and propositions and proofs connecting the framework to Hilbert-space operator-valued Gaussian processes.

C1.justification: The central post-hoc linearization, function-valued GP and scalability claims remain. V2 reframes the Laplace-centered presentation as the broader LUNO framework and explicitly accommodates non-Gaussian random processes. Compatibility with alternative Gaussian inference schemes was already acknowledged in v1.

C2.justification: V1 discusses modest empirical gains and future interpolation-error investigations. V2 adds explanations of ensemble covariance rank deficiencies and rollout error accumulation, qualifies rank claims for numerical singularities, and identifies weight-space covariance modeling as the main limitation. It also distinguishes ensemble advantages in next-step prediction from their rollout uncertainty weaknesses.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds substantial reproducibility information absent from v1: APEBench and custom PDE-generation procedures, solver and grid details, training epochs, AdamW and scheduling, JAX/Flax/Optax, padding, rank-500 GGN approximation, and a 500-point calibration grid. These are documented details, not evidence that every underlying implementation choice changed.

R1.justification: Literature coverage expands across FNO theory and applications, active learning, Bayesian optimization, probabilistic numerics, ensembles and operator-GP methods. V1 distinguishes its Banach setting from earlier Hilbert-space work; v2 develops an explicit embedding relationship with the Owhadi/Batlle frameworks in Appendix A.5.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and conclusion are substantially rewritten, with NOLA renamed LUNO and Gaussian currying reframed as probabilistic currying. Laplace background moves from Section 2.3 to Appendix B, the detailed FNO derivation moves to Appendix C, and experimental documentation is reorganized into Appendix D.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one column to two. The overview diagram is relocated and relabeled, while experimental displays are extensively redesigned with covariance/eigenfunction panels, spatial residual maps, rollout curves, and new dataset, OOD and runtime tables.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicitly acknowledged need for more diverse, multidimensional tests and substantially strengthens comparisons through ensembles and matched sampling-versus-linearization controls. OOD, covariance and rollout analyses make benefits and failure modes more assessable, while detailed experimental appendices improve reproducibility. Losing the training-size sweep and introducing some table-label and timing-reporting ambiguities are limited drawbacks relative to these gains.
